title: Welcome to FPL Tracker
summary: A 60-second tour of what this app is, what your league lives on it, and where to look first.
body: FPL Tracker is a private analytics dashboard for your Fantasy Premier League mini-league. It pulls live data from the official FPL API, layers your league's standings on top of it, and unpacks the bits FPL doesn't expose — bench waste, captain regrets, transfer hits, head-to-head comparisons, and a deliberately petty Wall of Shame. There is no public mode. Every page is gated behind a sign-in, and every member sees only the league(s) they belong to. What you can do here - Read the league. Standings, live points, transfers, ownership, form, captain history — every page is one click from the sidebar. - Compare yourself. Head-to-head, captain what-ifs, transfer regret, bench waste — quantify exactly where you went wrong. - Track the season. Cumulative stats, agony index, luck ranking, Wall of Shame trophy cards that update every gameweek. - Stay in the loop. Optional weekly digest email summarises the gameweek with manager-by-manager commentary. Where to look first If you're brand new, the natural reading order is: 1. Standings — the home leaderboard. Start here to recognise who's who. 2. Live Points — mid-gameweek tracker. Bookmark it for Saturday afternoons. 3. Form Table — last-three-gameweek momentum. Whose run is real, whose is regression-to-the-mean. 4. Bench Waste — the heatmap of cumulative pain. If you've just been invited as a League Admin, the League Admin overview is your starting point instead. The sidebar is your friend. Sections collapse and expand; the page you're currently on is highlighted in green. The "Help" entry brings you back here. Where the data comes from Standings, live points, transfers, fixtures, player metadata — everything time-sensitive is fetched live from the official Fantasy Premier League API. Your league's roster and admin settings live in this app's database. Both layers refresh on a sensible cadence, and stale data is signalled with a small "refreshing…" pill on the affected page rather than silently leaving yesterday's numbers in place. What this app is NOT It isn't a replacement for the official FPL site — you still pick your team there. It isn't a public social network — no posts, no DMs, no public leaderboards. It isn't betting infrastructure — there's no integration with bookmakers, no odds, no payouts, no money handling.

title: Signing in with a magic-link
summary: There are no passwords. Enter your email, click the link we send you, and you're in.
body: Sign-in is passwordless. You enter your email on the sign-in page, we email you a one-time link, and clicking the link signs you in for the next thirty days on that device. There is no password to remember, no password to lose, no password to be stolen. The flow Visit — or just visit any page on the app while signed out and you'll be redirected there. Enter the email associated with your league membership. Within about thirty seconds, you should see an email titled "Sign in to FPL Tracker" from your league's configured sender address. It contains a single big "Sign in" button. Clicking the button opens the app, validates the token, and signs you in. You'll land on the standings page of your league (or, if you belong to multiple leagues, the league chooser). How long the link lives The magic-link is valid for 15 minutes after it's sent and can only be used once. If you click it after that, or click it a second time, the app will tell you the link has expired and offer to send a fresh one. This window is deliberately short — magic-links are credentials, and a credential that lives forever is a credential someone can find later. Fifteen minutes is plenty for the round-trip from "request" to "click", and short enough that an intercepted link is useless soon after. Forwarding the link to someone else is the same as forwarding your password. If they click it before you, they're signed in as you and you're not. If you ever forward by accident, sign yourself out via the sidebar's "Sign out" button — that invalidates every session on every device — then request a fresh link. How long the session lives Once you're signed in, the session cookie lasts 30 days with a sliding refresh — every visit resets the clock. You won't have to re-authenticate during normal use. You will have to re-authenticate after thirty days of inactivity, after explicitly signing out, or after clearing your browser cookies. What if the link doesn't arrive? See Troubleshooting sign-in. The short version: check your spam folder first, ask your league admin to confirm your email is on file, then ask for a fresh link.

title: Switching between leagues
summary: If you're in more than one league, the League Switcher at the top of the sidebar moves you between them while keeping your context.
body: The platform supports multiple leagues per account. If you're a member or admin of more than one, you can flip between them without signing out. How to switch Click the league name at the top of the sidebar. A dropdown opens showing every active league you belong to. Selecting one navigates you to the equivalent page in that league. For example: if you're on and pick "Sea Eagles" from the dropdown, you'll land at . Page context is preserved. Admin context is preserved too If you're a League Admin in multiple leagues, the switcher behaves more cleverly. From , picking "Sea Eagles" — where you're also an admin — lands you at , not the standings page. You stay in the same admin sub-shell across leagues. If you switch to a league where you're only a member (not an admin), the switcher drops you off at for that league instead. When you only have one league If your account belongs to exactly one active league, there's no switcher — the sidebar just shows that league's name. You'll only ever see the switcher once a second active membership exists. Where the chooser shows up After sign-in, if you belong to more than one league, you'll land on — a one-time chooser with all your leagues partitioned into "Leagues you administer" and "Leagues you're a member of" (if you have both). After you pick one, you go straight into it; the in-app switcher takes over from there. Every URL includes a league slug. Sharing with another Sandsharks member opens correctly for them. Sharing it with someone who isn't in Sandsharks returns 404 — deliberate non-disclosure; we don't reveal that the league exists.

title: Accepting an invitation
summary: You received an invitation email from your league admin. Here's what to do with it.
body: When a League Admin invites you, you'll receive an email containing a unique acceptance link. Clicking it takes you to a page that confirms which league you're joining, optionally collects your FPL Manager ID, and signs you in. The flow The email has a single "Accept invitation" button. Clicking it opens in your browser. The page shows the league name + logo and your role (member or admin). If your league admin didn't pre-link your FPL Manager ID, you'll be asked for it now. You can find your Manager ID by visiting your FPL points page and copying the number from the URL. Accepting creates your account if you don't already have one, attaches the membership to your account, signs you in, and lands you on the league's standings page. How long the invitation lives Invitations are single-use and expire 7 days after they're issued. If you miss the window, the link will tell you it's expired and ask you to contact your league admin for a fresh invitation. An invitation link is single-use, but it doesn't verify who clicked it. If you forward the email and someone else clicks first, they take your spot. Open it on a device only you have access to. What if you already have an account? If the email matches an existing UserAccount, accepting the invitation just attaches the new membership to your existing account. Next time you sign in, the LeagueSwitcher will show the new league alongside any you already had. What if your league admin made a mistake? If the email address on the invitation is wrong (e.g. you should be using your work email but the invitation went to a personal address), don't accept it. Ask the admin to revoke the invitation and issue a new one to the correct email. Accepting under the wrong email creates a UserAccount under that wrong email, which is fixable but annoying.

title: Troubleshooting sign-in
summary: The magic-link didn't arrive, or arrived and didn't work. Here's the checklist.
body: The magic-link flow is short, but a handful of things can go wrong. Work through this list in order. The link never arrived Magic-link emails are transactional, but spam filters are not perfect. Search your inbox for "FPL Tracker" or for the sender address your league uses. If you find it in spam, mark it "not spam" so future links land in the inbox. The platform only emails addresses that have a UserAccount or a pending invitation. If you signed in with the wrong email — for example a personal address when your invitation was sent to your work address — no email was ever sent. The sign-in form deliberately shows the same "if an account exists, we sent a link" message either way, to avoid revealing which addresses have accounts. Ask your League Admin (or a Super Admin) to confirm which email is on your membership. Delivery is normally within ~30 seconds but can occasionally stretch to a minute. If nothing appears, request a fresh link by re-submitting the sign-in form. In dev / staging environments, magic-links are printed to the server console instead of emailed. If your league deployment is on a host where SMTP is misconfigured, no email will go out. The admin can check the server logs to confirm. The link arrived but doesn't work Clicking a magic-link a second time, or clicking it more than fifteen minutes after it was issued, won't sign you in — the token is intentionally one-shot and short-lived. If you see a "Link expired" message: 1. Just go back to and request a fresh link. There's no penalty. 2. If you suspect someone else clicked it first (e.g. you forwarded the email), sign out from any other device and request a new link. If you see "Link invalid" without ever clicking before: 1. The email link may have been mangled by your mail client (some break long URLs across lines). Try copy-pasting the entire URL into your browser address bar manually. 2. If still broken, request a fresh link from . I keep getting signed out Sessions last 30 days with a sliding window — every visit resets the clock. If you're being signed out repeatedly, the likely causes are: - Cookie clearing — browser privacy settings or extensions that wipe cookies on close. - Multiple devices — signing in on a new device doesn't sign you out elsewhere, but explicitly clicking "Sign out" in the sidebar invalidates every session you have, everywhere. - 30 days of inactivity — if you genuinely haven't visited in a month, the session lapsed. I lost access to my email The platform has no "I forgot my email" recovery. Email IS the credential. If you no longer have access to the email tied to your membership: 1. Ask a League Admin to update your email on file via . They can change your address; you can then sign in via the new one. 2. If you're the only admin and you've lost your own email access, ask a Super Admin to either change your email directly or to issue a fresh invitation to a recoverable address.

title: Standings
summary: The home leaderboard. Total points, gameweek points, rank, and rank-change for every member of your league.
body: Standings is your league's leaderboard — every member ranked by total points with their latest gameweek score, captain pick, chip usage, and rank-change indicators. What each column means | Column | What it shows | |---|---| | # | Current rank in the league. Rank 1 is the leader by total points. | | ▲ / ▼ | Rank change since the previous gameweek. Green up-arrow = you climbed; red down-arrow = you dropped. | | Manager / Team | The member's display name and FPL team name. Click the name to open their member profile. | | GW Points | Points scored in the currently-selected gameweek. The default is the live or most-recently-completed GW. | | Total | Cumulative season points. | | Behind | How many points behind the leader. Always 0 for the leader. | | Captain | The captain pick for the selected GW, with that player's points (×2, or ×3 for the Triple Captain). | | Chip | Any chip played in the selected GW (Wildcard, Free Hit, Bench Boost, Triple Captain). Empty means no chip. | The gameweek selector The selector in the top-right of the page lets you jump to any prior gameweek. The leaderboard re-sorts and the rank-change arrows recompute against the previous GW (not the current one). This is how you compare snapshots over the season without leaving the page. The Points Race chart Above the leaderboard, the chart shows cumulative total points for every manager across every gameweek so far. The leader's line is slightly bolder; a dashed reference line marks the currently-selected GW. Hover any point to see who was where. The Relegation Zone If your league has four or more managers, the bottom three rows are styled as a relegation zone: red-tinted backgrounds, a "DANGER" badge, and a colour-coded depth bar at the bottom of each row (amber → red the further down you are). A dashed ⚠️ separator divides "safe" from "drop zone". This is purely cosmetic — there's no actual relegation happening — but it's where the GW Punishment Suggester reads from. The bottom scorer of each gameweek gets sentenced to one of a rotating list of forfeits. League Admins can apply a per-manager per-gameweek points deduction (for late deadlines, missed digests, whatever house rules apply). Deductions show up as a reduced GW Points value with a small badge — see Edit a member. Where the data comes from Standings comes from the FPL API, filtered to your league's actual roster. Sorting, rank-change, and the average-points reference values are computed live by this app — they're not cached longer than ~60 seconds during a live gameweek, and a "refreshing…" pill surfaces the moment the cached value is stale.

title: Live Points
summary: Mid-gameweek tracker. Every manager's live score updated as fixtures play out.
body: The Live Points page is what you have open in another tab on Saturday afternoons. It shows every manager's points as fixtures play out, including provisional bonus points, autosubs, and captain doublings — all the things the official FPL site shows on its own live page, but consolidated for your league. What's on the page - Live total per manager — the same number you'd see on FPL's live page, computed against your league's roster. - Players still to play — count of starting-eleven players whose fixture hasn't kicked off yet. - Provisional bonus — the bonus points FPL is currently allocating; locks in at full-time of each match. - Captain badge — the captain pick and their live multiplier (×2 normal, ×3 Triple Captain). - Chip indicator — Bench Boost players are included in the live total; Triple Captain is reflected in the captain badge. How fresh is "live" The page polls the FPL API on a short cycle (typically every 60 seconds during in-progress gameweeks). A "refreshing…" pill appears in the header whenever the cached value is more than ~60 seconds old; the data underneath swaps in once the refresh completes. You don't have to hit reload manually. When no gameweek is in progress (between deadline and the first kickoff, or after every fixture finishes), the page falls back to showing the most recent completed gameweek's points alongside an "All fixtures complete" banner. Autosubs If your starter doesn't play (didn't appear in the matchday squad, or was an unused substitute who came on for a player who got 0 minutes), the FPL engine automatically substitutes in your highest-priority bench player who DID play. Those autosubs are reflected in the live total here as soon as FPL's API updates them — typically within minutes of the relevant fixture ending. If your captain doesn't appear in the matchday squad, your vice-captain becomes the live captain (×2). If neither plays, you get a single multiplier on whoever did. The live total reflects this automatically. What this page doesn't show - It doesn't show per-player breakdowns — go to the official FPL live page for that. - It doesn't show historical gameweeks — use Standings with the GW selector instead. - It doesn't show fixture scores — go to Fixtures for those.

title: Transfers
summary: Who bought and sold whom, when, and how many hits they took to do it.
body: The Transfers page logs every transfer every member has made this season — player in, player out, cost in points hits, and the gameweek the transfer was made for. What you see For each manager, a list of transfers in chronological order (newest first): - In / Out — the players bought and sold, with their current price. - GW — the gameweek the transfer was made for. Note: a transfer made on Friday for GW 27 shows GW 27 here, not the calendar week it was made in. - Hit — if the manager spent more than their free transfers, they took a -4 hit per extra transfer. The total cost is shown as , , etc. - Net result — combined points scored by the new player(s) over the points the sold player(s) would have scored, minus the hit cost. This is the realisation of the gamble. What it tells you A glance at this page lets you see: - Who plays aggressively (lots of transfers) vs. set-and-forget (rare moves). - Who routinely takes hits, and whether those hits paid off (positive net result) or backfired (negative). - Who panic-traded in to chase last week's points (transferred in a player AFTER their big haul), and whether it cost them. Wildcard and Free Hit transfers Transfers made during a Wildcard or Free Hit are shown but flagged as such. The hit cost is zero on those weeks (the chip removes the penalty). Free Hit reverses the next week — the players sold come back and the players bought go away — so the realised value of a Free Hit transfer is unusual to compute and is left off the net-result column for those rows. Transfers shows you what happened. Transfer Regret ranks the same moves by how badly they aged. Open both side-by-side after a chaotic gameweek. Refresh cadence Transfers data is fetched on a longer cycle than live points — typically every 5 minutes — because it only changes at the gameweek deadline. The "refreshing…" pill appears when the cached value is older than that.

title: Form Table
summary: Last-three-gameweek momentum, with inline sparklines showing whose trend is real.
body: The Form Table re-ranks your league by recent performance rather than season total. Each manager's last three gameweek scores are averaged, and the table sorts by that average — so the manager who's been clobbering it for three GWs surfaces at the top regardless of their overall standing. What each column means | Column | What it shows | |---|---| | Form rank | Position by 3-GW average score. Top = best recent form. | | Manager | Display name + team. | | GW-2, GW-1, GW | The actual scores from the last three completed gameweeks. | | Avg (3) | The average of those three. | | Trend | Inline SVG sparkline connecting the three dots. Green = improving, red = declining, grey = flat. | | Overall rank | Their position in the season-long Standings, for context. | How to read the trend The sparkline does what tables don't: it shows you direction. A manager averaging 60 might be 30 → 60 → 90 (sharp recovery) or 90 → 60 → 30 (sharp decline) — same average, totally different stories. The colour of the line tells you which: - Green — the last GW is higher than the first of the three. Momentum is up. - Red — the last GW is lower than the first. Momentum is down. - Grey — flat or near-flat. No clear direction. The area under the line is subtly tinted to reinforce the direction. Why this matters Total points are the only thing that decides a season, but recent form is what predicts the next few weeks. A manager riding a 90 → 95 → 100 streak is probably making smart choices that will compound; a 60 → 50 → 40 manager is probably leaking points to bench picks and broken captains. If you spot a sudden decline on the Form Table, open Captain History for that manager. Bad captain picks for three weeks running are the most common explanation.

title: Season Stats
summary: League-wide cumulative numbers — total bench wasted, total transfer hits, total captain blanks, and more.
body: Season Stats is the dashboard view of the league's collective season so far. It rolls up every gameweek into a single screen of cumulative totals and per-manager breakdowns, so you can see at a glance whose habits have cost them the most. What's on the page The page splits into three bands: League totals (top): single-number cards summing across every member — - Total bench points wasted across the season - Total points paid in transfer hits - Total captain blanks (captain scored ≤ 3) - Average gameweek score across all managers, all weeks Per-manager breakdown (middle): each manager's individual contribution to each total, sortable by column. Trends (bottom): cumulative line charts for each metric so you can see whether the league is getting better or worse over time. (Spoiler: usually worse.) What each metric counts - Bench points wasted — points scored by your bench players that you didn't get because they weren't in your starting eleven. Autosubs that DO trigger don't count — those are points you got. - Transfer hits — the -4 (or -8, etc.) penalties for transfers above the free allowance. Chip-protected transfers (Wildcard, Free Hit) don't count. - Captain blanks — gameweeks where your captain scored 3 or fewer points (after the multiplier is applied). A failed Triple Captain is especially painful here. - Average GW score — total GW points across all members divided by (members × completed GWs). How it relates to the other pages This page is the executive summary. Each metric has a dedicated deep-dive elsewhere: - Bench detail → Bench Waste - Transfer detail → Transfer Regret - Captain detail → Captain History and Captain What-If - A composite of all three → Agony Index Use Season Stats to spot anomalies; click through to the dedicated page when you want the story behind the number. Season Stats updates as soon as the previous gameweek's data finalises in the FPL API — typically Tuesday afternoon UK time after Monday-night fixtures and bonus-point recalculation finish.

title: Bench Waste
summary: A manager-by-gameweek heatmap of points left rotting on your bench.
body: The Bench Waste page surfaces the saddest stat in FPL: points your players scored while sitting on your bench, doing nothing for your team total. The page is a heatmap — managers as rows, gameweeks as columns — with each cell shaded by how many points were wasted that week. How to read the heatmap - Cell colour intensity goes pale gold → orange → deep red as bench points climb. - Red outline on a cell marks that manager's personal worst gameweek of the season. - Total column on the right is each manager's cumulative bench waste so far. - Total row at the bottom is the league's collective bench waste per gameweek. GW columns turn red when the league as a whole left a lot on the bench that week. Hover any cell to see the exact points wasted, the GW number, and the manager's name. On mobile, tap to reveal the same tooltip. What counts as "wasted" Bench points wasted = points scored by a player on your bench whom you did NOT replace via an autosub. The FPL engine autosubs in a bench player when one of your starting eleven doesn't play (zero minutes); when that happens, those points are not wasted — you got them. So "wasted" specifically means: - Your bench player scored points - Your starting eleven all played at least one minute (or were captain/vice and got a captain rule) - Therefore, no autosub happened, and the bench points didn't count Bench Boost weeks count zero bench waste — everyone played. Why this is the most painful page Bench waste compounds. Five points missed in GW 1 is annoying; the same five points missed every week is 200 by season's end. The cumulative column tells you the real cost of consistently choosing the wrong starters. A manager can win a gameweek and still leave 30 points on the bench. Don't confuse "high score" with "well-managed team" — the heatmap will tell you who's getting away with sloppy bench choices on a good week.

title: Captain History
summary: Every captain pick from every manager across every gameweek, colour-coded by points.
body: The Captain History page is a grid of every captain pick in the league for every completed gameweek. Cell colour tells you the points the captain scored (after multiplier); the most popular pick each gameweek is highlighted. How to read it - Columns are gameweeks (oldest left, current right). - Rows are managers in season-rank order. - Cells show the captain's surname (or shorter form for long names) on a coloured background. - Cell colour scales by post-multiplier points: pale grey ≤ 5, soft green for 6-9, green for 10-15, deep green for 16+. - Triple Captain weeks get a distinctive border so you can spot the gambles. Hover a cell to see the full player name, the GW number, the raw score, and the multiplier applied. What it tells you - Cluster columns — when most of the league captains the same player, you'll see a stripe of identical names. These are the obvious picks (Salah, Haaland, Saka). Differential captains stand out because they break the stripe. - Personal patterns — scan a row and you'll see which managers chase last week's hauler vs. which read fixtures vs. which always go to the captain of the on-form-team. - Triple Captain decisions — the bordered cells are the gambles. Did each manager play their TC on a 30-pointer or a 6-pointer? Captain History shows what each manager did. Captain What-If shows what they should have done. Open them side by side after every gameweek. Captaincy stats card Above the grid, a summary card surfaces league-wide captaincy facts: - The most-captained player of the season - The highest single-GW captain return (player + manager + score) - The biggest captain blank (player + manager + score) - The success rate of differential captain picks across the league

title: H2H Battle Simulator
summary: Pit any two managers against each other in any gameweek and see who would have won.
body: The H2H Battle Simulator takes two managers and any single gameweek, then shows the full head-to-head: starting elevens, differential picks, captain choices, and the score line that would have settled it. How to use it Two dropdowns at the top of the page. You can pick any two — including yourself vs. the leader, or two of your rivals. Defaults to the most recently completed GW. Use the selector to step back through the season. The page renders two columns — one per manager — with their starting elevens, captain pick, bench, chip used (if any), and the final score line at the bottom. What's highlighted Differentials — players one manager owns and the other doesn't are marked with a coloured border in the column of whoever owns them. This is where the matchup was actually decided. Captain picks — both captain badges are shown prominently. If they captained the same player, the multipliers cancel; if they captained different players, the captain who outscored the other wins this micro-battle on the page. Chip indicators — Wildcard, Free Hit, Bench Boost, and Triple Captain are all flagged. Note that a Bench Boost extends the starting eleven to 15. Why it's useful - Post-mortem — settle "what if we'd played each other this week" arguments definitively. - Style comparison — see at a glance whose teams are riskier (more differentials) vs. more template (mostly the same picks as everyone else). - Bragging rights — if you'd beaten the leader four weeks in a row but had a bad GW 1, this page is your evidence. What this page doesn't simulate It doesn't simulate the FPL H2H scoring format (1 for a draw, 3 for a win across a fixed schedule). This is just total-points head-to-head for the selected gameweek. If your league runs the official H2H format, the standings reflect that elsewhere — this page is a pure points comparison.

title: Transfer Regret
summary: For every transfer, the player you sold, the player you bought, and the points difference that followed.
body: Transfer Regret ranks every single transfer in the league by how much it cost (or earned) the manager who made it. The metric is brutally simple: from the gameweek of the transfer onward, how many points did the player you sold score vs. how many points did the player you bought score? Negative numbers are the regrets. What each column means | Column | What it shows | |---|---| | Manager | Who made the transfer. | | GW | The gameweek the transfer was made for. | | Out | The player sold, and their points scored from this GW onward. | | In | The player bought, and their points scored from this GW onward. | | Hit | -4 per excess transfer. Wildcard / Free Hit transfers show "(free)". | | Net | − − . Negative = regret. The colour intensifies (red) as the regret grows. | How to read it The table defaults to sorting by Net ascending — biggest regrets first. The transfers at the top of the page are the ones where someone sold a player who then went on a rampage and bought a player who promptly got injured. You can re-sort by: - Manager — group all of one manager's transfers together. - GW — see all transfers chronologically. - Hit — the hits that backfired hardest. A transfer made in GW 5 is still accumulating regret in GW 20 if the player sold is still scoring more than the player bought. The Net column reflects the season's total damage from that single decision, not just the week after. What this doesn't measure - Opportunity cost — if you transferred A out for B, but C would have been the better buy, the regret only compares A vs. B, not A vs. C. - Cascading transfers — if you sold a player to free up budget for another move, the page treats them as separate transfers, not a package. - Wildcard transfers — these are listed but flagged as free; the Net is computed on player swap only. For a more holistic "what was your worst move ever" rank, see the Wall of Shame, which surfaces the single worst transfer of the season as a trophy.

title: Agony Index
summary: A composite misfortune score that rolls bench waste, transfer hits, captain blanks, and gameweek suffering into a single leaderboard nobody wants to top.
body: The Agony Index is the dark mirror of the Standings page. It ranks managers not by points scored but by points wasted — and weights the different kinds of waste so the leaderboard reflects who has suffered most. The formula Each component contributes to the total. The mix matters as much as the total — two managers can have the same agony score with completely different stories underneath. Reading the stacked bar Above the leaderboard, the page shows a horizontal stacked bar per manager, with each segment colour-coded by component: - Slate — bench points wasted - Amber — transfer hits - Red — captain blanks - Purple — below-average gameweek suffering The longest bar is at the top. The legend shows the league-wide total for each component so you can see where your collective league pain comes from. Per-manager breakdown Below the leaderboard, each manager has a card showing: - Their agony rank and total - A breakdown of each component - Their worst single-GW incident in each category — "GW 12 — bench scored 22", "GW 19 — Salah captained for 2 points", "GW 7 — minus 8 transfer hit, gained 1 point" What it's good for - Identifying habits — a manager with high bench waste but low transfer hits is a "set-and-forget who picks the wrong starters". A manager with the opposite is a "constant tinkerer". Both bad, both diagnosable. - Reading the league's collective pain — the stacked-bar visualisation tells you whether your league is a transfer-hit-heavy league or a bench-waste-heavy one. Useful for designing house rules. - Bragging rights — being top of the Standings AND bottom of the Agony Index is the cleanest possible season. Being bottom of Standings AND top of Agony is, well, the wooden spoon plus. The "below-average GW suffering" component only counts each GW once per manager. If you scored 60 in a week when the league averaged 65, that's 5 agony points from that week. It's not a cumulative-deficit metric.

title: Luck Ranking
summary: Separates skill from luck by comparing your actual gameweek scores to a model of what you "should" have scored.
body: The Luck Ranking tries to answer the most contentious question in FPL: am I good or am I lucky? It does this by building a per-manager expected-points baseline (xPts) from the underlying FPL data — minutes, expected goals/assists, bonus probability — and comparing your actual points against that expectation. What the ranking shows Each manager has three numbers and a delta: - Actual points — your real season total. - Expected points (xPts) — what your team should have scored based on the underlying chances created, minutes played, and shot quality. - Δ — actual minus expected. Positive means you got more than your team's underlying performance suggested (you've been lucky); negative means you got less (you've been unlucky). - Luck rank — 1 = luckiest, last = unluckiest. Independent of the Standings rank. The page sorts by Δ descending — luckiest manager at the top, unluckiest at the bottom. How xPts is calculated For each player you own, in each gameweek: - Expected minutes from FPL's projected lineup data - Expected goals + assists from underlying shot quality (xG/xA) - Expected appearance, clean sheet, and goal-conceded contributions - Expected captain multiplier applied to your actual captain These get summed across your starting eleven (or 15 for Bench Boost weeks). Bonus is approximated from BPS expectation rather than awarded explicitly. This isn't a true model of FPL — it's a heuristic. But over a full season it's a much better signal of "how well did you pick" than total points alone, because points are noisy and xPts smooths the noise out. If you're in the top 3 by points AND ranked 8th by luck (meaning you've been more unlucky than most), you're playing genuinely well. If you're top 3 by points and 1st by luck (meaning the dice landed in your favour all season), enjoy it while it lasts — that's regression to the mean waiting to happen. What the model can't see - Differential picks that work — if you correctly identified a low-owned player who outperformed his xPts, you'll appear lucky even though it was insight. Pure-stats models can't tell genius from variance. - Chip timing — playing your Bench Boost on the right double-gameweek is a skill the model rates as "lucky" because all 15 of your starters scored. - Knowing when to take a hit — a successful -4 for an injury replacement looks like luck to the model. So treat the Luck rank as a conversation starter, not a verdict.

title: Captain What-If
summary: For every gameweek, what your captain scored vs. the best captain you could have picked from your own squad.
body: Captain What-If quantifies the cost of every captain pick. For each gameweek, it compares what your actual captain scored (after multiplier) against what your best owned alternative would have scored. The gap is the points you left on the table. How to use it Defaults to you. The dropdown lets you analyse any league member. Optimal picks count, total misses, biggest single-GW miss, and average miss per GW. Green = you picked the optimal captain. Amber = small miss (≤4 pts). Orange = moderate (≤10 pts). Red = catastrophic (>10 pts). Below the chart, the per-GW breakdown table shows your captain (with points), the best alternative you owned (with points), and the score impact. What "best alternative" means The page considers only players that were in your squad that gameweek — including bench players. The "best alternative" is whoever scored highest. So if you captained Salah for 8 and a bench midfielder you owned scored 18, the miss is . Ouch. This is the realistic ceiling — captaincy is a choice between players you actually owned. The page doesn't compare against players you didn't own (that would be the global ceiling, a different and arguably more painful number). Triple Captain weeks If you played Triple Captain that week, the multiplier is 3 instead of 2 for both the actual and the hypothetical. The page reflects this in the GW row. Why this matters Captain points are roughly 20% of your weekly score on average. Optimising captaincy is the single highest-leverage decision you make each week. A manager who consistently picks the optimal captain (green bars all season) is doing one thing extraordinarily well, even if everything else is mediocre. The page shows the optimal pick after the fact. The point is to identify patterns over time — e.g. you systematically captain the wrong forward when there's a rotation risk. Picking on a single bad GW is not a strategy.

title: Wall of Shame
summary: Six permanent trophy cards for the season's most spectacular failures, updated every gameweek.
body: The Wall of Shame is the season's permanent record of the worst moments. Six awards, six trophy cards, one current holder each. The awards update every gameweek as the season progresses — and the awkward truth is that some holders never change, while others trade hands week to week. The six awards 🪑 The Bench Warmer For the most cumulative bench points wasted across the season. This is the slow-burn award — it doesn't change much from week to week, it just slowly compounds. The Bench Warmer is the manager who consistently picks the wrong starting eleven. 🩸 The Masochist Medal For the most points paid in transfer hits across the season. Awarded for self-inflicted damage — every -4 you took voluntarily, summed. A high score here means a manager who genuinely cannot leave their team alone. 🥄 The Wooden Spoon For the lowest single-gameweek score of the season. Changes hands whenever someone has a truly catastrophic week. Defending the wooden spoon is impressive; reclaiming it from yourself is concerning. 🔥 The Bonfire of Vanities For the worst single-gameweek bench waste. Different from the Bench Warmer (which is cumulative) — this is the one week you really should have started the kid from the U23s. ©️ The Armband of Doom For the worst captain blank by raw post-multiplier points. Captain scoring 2 means -8 from the doubled total. Triple Captain scoring 1 is -10. The Armband of Doom is whichever pick stings the most. 🤡 The Regret Machine For the season's single worst transfer. Shows the player sold, the player bought, and the cumulative point delta from the gameweek of the transfer onward. The card surfaces the FULL trade — including the hit cost if any. Sidebar — Hall of Repeat Offenders Below the main grid, a sidebar lists managers who have held two or more awards simultaneously at any point in the season. It's a small honour. How awards update Every gameweek the page recomputes from scratch. There are no "frozen" historic holders — if you got the Wooden Spoon in GW 3 but someone scored lower in GW 17, the title transfers. The page reads from the same data as the analytics pages; updates land within minutes of the previous GW's bonus points finalising. At the end of each gameweek, screenshot the Wall of Shame and post it to your league's group chat. Public shaming is healthy in moderation.

title: Fixtures
summary: The next five gameweeks of fixtures, sorted by team, with FPL difficulty ratings and live scores.
body: The Fixtures page is your transfer-planning surface. It shows the next five upcoming gameweeks for every Premier League team in a single grid, colour-coded by FPL's difficulty rating, so you can see at a glance who has the kindest run-in. How to read the grid - Rows — every Premier League team, sorted by their current league position. - Columns — the next five gameweeks starting from the current one. - Cells — the opponent + (H) for home / (A) for away, on a coloured background. The colour scale matches FPL's official difficulty rating (FDR): | Rating | Colour | Meaning | |---|---|---| | 1 (easiest) | Deep green | Should beat them comfortably | | 2 | Light green | Favourites | | 3 | Grey | Even matchup | | 4 | Light red | Tough fixture | | 5 (hardest) | Deep red | Title-contender opponent away | Live scores During an in-progress gameweek, the current GW column shows live scores instead of fixture difficulty. Final scores remain on the grid for ~24 hours after the gameweek ends before reverting to the difficulty-rating view. The page polls FPL for live scores on a 60-second cycle while fixtures are in progress. The "refreshing…" pill in the page header surfaces when the cached data is stale. Double and blank gameweeks When a team plays twice in a single GW (a "double gameweek"), both opponents appear in the same cell. When a team has no fixture (a "blank gameweek"), the cell is empty and styled differently to flag it. These are the weeks where chips matter most: - Bench Boost in a double-gameweek = 11 → 15 players × 2 fixtures = a lot of upside. - Free Hit in a blank-gameweek = field a full team of players who DO have a fixture. - Wildcard before a stretch of doubles = restructure to lean into the upside. FDR is a rough guide. It doesn't know about injuries, suspensions, or recent form. Use it to spot patterns, not to make absolute decisions.

title: Ownership
summary: For every player owned by anyone in your league, how many of your managers own them.
body: The Ownership page lists every player owned by at least one manager in your league, along with how many managers own them. It's the mirror of FPL's global ownership percentages — but scoped to your league, which is the comparison that actually matters for league position. What the columns mean | Column | What it shows | |---|---| | Player | Name, club, and position. | | Owned by | How many managers in your league own this player out of the total. | | % | Same as Owned by, expressed as a percentage of the league. | | Owners | The list of managers who own them, displayed as chips. | | GW pts | The player's points in the most recent completed gameweek. | | Total pts | Their season total. | The table is sortable by any column. Default sort is Owned by descending — the league's template players are at the top. Reading the league's template The top of the table is your league's "template" — the players most managers own. Owning the template is comfortable; it means you can't fall behind on any given week because everyone else gets the same points from those players. Below the template, ownership thins out. The middle of the table is where most of the variance happens: players owned by some, not by others. This is where the league is won and lost. The bottom of the table — players owned by 1 or 2 managers — is the "differentials" zone. See the dedicated Differentials page for an alternative cut of this data. What to do with this information - Spot opportunities — a player on top form whom most of the league DOESN'T own is a transfer-in opportunity for you to gain on the field. - Hedge against risk — a heavily-owned player about to be benched or rotated is a risk for the league but also a chance for you to differentiate by NOT owning them. - Plan captaincy — when most of the league captains the same player, your captaincy choices have less impact. When ownership is fragmented, captain choice swings results. The Ownership page shows ownership as of the most recently completed gameweek. Transfers made in the current GW won't reflect here until that GW finalises. Use Transfers for real-time activity.

title: Differential Alerts
summary: Low-owned players who scored big in the most recent gameweek — the players that decided the GW.
body: A differential is a player only some managers own. If they score big, they swing the gameweek. The Differential Alerts page surfaces the differentials that mattered most this gameweek — low-owned players who delivered. What's on the page The page is a table of differential picks from the most recent completed gameweek, sorted by impact (points × inverse ownership). Each row shows: - Player — name, club, position. - GW points — what they scored in the gameweek (before captain multiplier). - Owned by — count and percentage of league managers who owned them. - Captained by — managers who captained them (these are the big winners). - Impact — composite score combining points and rarity. Higher = bigger differential. The default filter shows players owned by 30% or fewer of the league. You can raise or lower that threshold with the slider at the top. What "impact" means A 15-point haul from a player owned by 1 of 12 managers is more meaningful than a 15-point haul from a player owned by 11 of 12. The first case is one manager getting a unique 15 points; the second is the whole league getting roughly the same boost. The Impact column rewards rarity: So: - 15 points, 8% ownership → ~13.8 impact - 15 points, 92% ownership → ~1.2 impact The same haul, vastly different effect on the league table. How to use it - Post-mortem — at the end of a gameweek, scan the top of the table. The managers listed in "Captained by" or "Owned by" are the ones who gained relative ground this week. - Transfer planning — a differential that scored big two weeks running is a candidate for transfer in before their ownership rises. The window closes fast. - Avoid the herd — high-impact differentials are easier to spot when ownership is fragmented. If everyone owns the same 11 players, there are no differentials. When a manager captains a low-owned differential and it pays off, they often jump multiple rank positions in a single GW. The "Captained by" column flags exactly when this is about to happen.

title: Injuries
summary: A list of every player owned by anyone in your league who has a non-100% chance of playing.
body: The Injuries page (called "Player Status" internally and labelled "Injuries" in the sidebar) lists every player owned by at least one manager in your league who is flagged in the FPL data with a less-than-100% chance of playing. It's your weekly watchlist — the players to keep an eye on before the deadline. How players appear here A player is flagged when FPL's API marks their chance of playing this round as something other than 100%. The values FPL uses are: | Chance | Meaning | |---|---| | 0% | Out — definitely not playing. | | 25% | Suspended or major doubt. | | 50% | Doubt. | | 75% | Likely to play, minor concern. | | Null / 100% | No issue flagged. (Not shown on this page.) | The page sorts by most owned first — the injury risks affecting the most managers surface at the top. What each column shows - Player — name, club, position. - Status — the textual reason from FPL ("Knee injury", "Match fitness", "Suspension"), if provided. - Chance — the numeric percentage from the table above. - Expected return — the date FPL projects the player will be available, if known. Many injury statuses don't have a return date and show "—". - Owned by — count and chips for the affected managers in your league. - News — the latest news snippet from FPL's API, if available. What to do with this Before every deadline: 1. Scan the top of the table. The most-owned doubts are where the league's collective risk sits. 2. Check the chance percentage. A 75% is usually fine; a 50% is a coin flip; a 25% or 0% requires action. 3. Plan substitutions. If your captain is on the list, set the vice. If a starter is on the list, check whether your bench has a viable autosub candidate. 4. Don't transfer reflexively. A short-term knock often clears by the next deadline. Use Transfers and Regret to gut-check whether you transfer in-and-out of injured players too often. FPL updates its API on Thursdays and Fridays before each gameweek. The flag for a player who picks up a knock in a Saturday match probably won't appear here until the following Thursday at the earliest. For real-time injury news, follow the club's media channels.

title: League Admin overview
summary: What you can do as a League Admin, where it lives in the app, and the order to learn things in.
body: You're a League Admin — you can configure your league, manage who's in it, send the weekly digest, and review the audit trail. This page is your map. What "League Admin" means You administer one or more leagues on this platform. The role grants you access to a per-league admin sub-shell at with four pages: - Settings — name, slug, logo, mini-league ID, and the digest prompt. - Members — sync from FPL, invite by email, edit individual member details. - Digest — send the weekly GW summary email to your league. - Audit log — every administrative action that has happened in your league, who did it, when. You do NOT have access to: - Platform-level admin (creating new leagues, suspending leagues, cross-league member views) — that's the Super Admin's purview. - The admin sub-shells of leagues you don't administer. - Any FPL system function (you can't take a hit on someone's team, you can't change their captain). Where to start If you've just been promoted: 1. League Settings — set the league name, upload a logo, paste your FPL mini-league ID. This is the one-time setup that makes everything else work. 2. Syncing members — pull every member of your mini-league into the app's roster. 3. Inviting members — turn those roster entries into signed-in users by inviting them by email. After that, the operational work is: - Sending the weekly digest — once per week, ideally after every fixture finishes. - Reading the audit log — only when you need to know "who changed X and when". The multi-admin entry point If you admin more than one league, the sidebar shows a "My admin leagues" link in addition to the per-league "Admin" sub-shell. That link goes to , where you get a list of every league you administer with deep-links straight into each one's sub-pages. The LeagueSwitcher also helps here — if you're on and switch to League B (where you're also admin), you land at , not the standings page. Admin context is preserved across switches. Settings + syncing + invitations are mostly one-time setup. The only routine admin task is sending the digest (and even that can be skipped some weeks). If you're touching admin pages every day, something's wrong — flag it to a Super Admin.

title: League settings
summary: Name, slug, logo, mini-league ID, digest prompt — every league-level configuration the platform exposes.
body: The League Settings page is your league's identity and integration layer. It's where you set the human-readable name, the URL slug, the optional logo, the FPL mini-league ID that powers member sync, and the AI tone prompt that flavours the weekly digest. The fields Name The human-readable name of your league — shown in the sidebar, on every email, on the invitation acceptance page, on the league chooser. Keep it short (≤60 chars) and recognisable. Slug The URL-safe identifier for your league. Appears in every URL: . Allowed: lowercase letters, digits, hyphens. Must be unique across the platform. When you change the slug, the old one is preserved in a redirect table so existing bookmarks keep working — old links 308 to the new slug automatically. But anything that hard-codes the old slug (e.g. someone's local notes) will need updating. Change slugs sparingly. Logo URL A URL to a logo image. If set, the logo appears: - In the sidebar under the platform brand block (a small thumbnail next to the league name). - On the invitation acceptance page, so invitees can confirm they're joining the right league. If you don't set one, those surfaces fall back gracefully (no badge). PNG or JPG works; recommended size 256×256 or larger, served over HTTPS. Mini-league ID The numeric ID of your FPL classic-format mini-league. Find it in the URL on the official FPL site: . This ID is what enables the "Sync members" action on the Members page — without it, syncing fails because the app doesn't know which FPL mini-league to fetch from. The platform enforces uniqueness — one mini-league can only be linked to one app-level League at a time. If you try to set a mini-league ID that's already linked elsewhere, you'll get a 409 error. Digest prompt Optional free-text prompt that customises the AI tone of the weekly digest email. Default: a neutral, friendly tone. Set it to something like "Write like a deadpan pub landlord" or "Cricket-commentary style, formal English" and the AI will adjust the manager-by-manager narratives accordingly. Empty is fine. The digest still sends; it just uses the default tone. What happens on save Every Save writes an showing the before/after diff for each changed field. Other admins (if you have more than one) can see exactly what changed and when on the Audit log. If you changed the slug, a row is created automatically so the old URL keeps working. No action required from you. What you CAN'T change here - Membership — managed on the Members page. - Active / suspended status — only Super Admins can suspend or reinstate. - Migration of the league to a different platform tenant — out of scope; ask a Super Admin.

title: Syncing members from FPL
summary: Pull your FPL mini-league's roster into the app in one click. Re-run whenever members come or go.
body: Once you've set the mini-league ID in League Settings, the Sync from League button on the Members admin page pulls every member of that mini-league into your app-level roster. What sync does When you click Sync: 1. The app calls the FPL API for your mini-league's full standings. 2. For each FPL manager in the result that doesn't already exist as a LeagueMembership in your league → create one. 3. For each existing LeagueMembership whose FPL manager has LEFT the mini-league (no longer in the FPL results) → mark inactive. 4. Manually-added members (those you added by email invitation, not via FPL sync) are left untouched — they're never auto-deactivated by sync. The result message shows: added: N, removed: M — so you can see at a glance what changed. What sync does NOT do - It does NOT send any emails. Newly-synced members exist in your roster but can't sign in until you explicitly invite them. See Inviting members. - It does NOT change any FPL-side data. Your mini-league on the official FPL site is the source of truth; this app reads from it. - It does NOT create UserAccounts. A LeagueMembership without a UserAccount means the manager appears in standings (their FPL points show up) but they can't sign in. When to run sync - Once during initial setup, after setting the mini-league ID. - Whenever a member joins or leaves your FPL mini-league. - Before sending the weekly digest, if members may have changed since the last digest. You don't need to run sync between every gameweek. The FPL API call to fetch standings happens on every page load anyway — sync is only about reconciling who exists in the app, not about refreshing points. This usually means someone joined your mini-league directly via FPL without going through the app's invitation flow. They appear because they're in the mini-league. Decide whether to invite them, ignore them, or remove them from the FPL mini-league entirely. What if sync fails The most common failures and what they mean: - "Mini-league ID not set" — go to League Settings and fill it in first. - "FPL API unavailable" — the official FPL API is having a moment. Wait a few minutes and try again. - "Mini-league not found" — the ID you set doesn't correspond to a real mini-league. Double-check by visiting in your browser. All failures are written to the audit log so you can see exactly when sync was attempted and what went wrong.

title: Inviting members by email
summary: Send a single-use magic-link to a new member so they can accept and sign in.
body: Members who exist in your roster (either via sync from FPL or added manually) can't sign in until they have a UserAccount linked to their membership. The invitation flow creates that link. The flow Sidebar → Admin → Members. Above the member table, you'll see an "Invite a member" button. - Email — the email address the invitation will go to. - Role — "Member" or "Admin". You can promote later, so default to Member unless you specifically want to share admin privileges. - FPL Manager ID (optional) — if you set this, the invitee skips the Manager ID field on the acceptance page. Use this when you already know which FPL manager they correspond to (e.g. they're already in your synced roster but have no email yet). The app creates an Invitation row, generates a single-use token valid for 7 days, and emails the link to the address you supplied. The audit log records the action. They click the link, optionally fill in their Manager ID (if you didn't pre-supply it), and accept. Their UserAccount is created (or linked, if one already exists for that email), the LeagueMembership is created (or its UserAccount is set), and they land on the league's standings page. Resending an invitation If the invitation expires or the recipient deletes the email, you can re-issue from the Members admin page. Each re-issue creates a fresh token; the old one becomes immediately invalid. The audit log records both the original issue and the re-issue. Cancelling an invitation Pending invitations (sent but not accepted) appear in a separate section of the Members page. You can revoke them; revocation invalidates the token immediately. If the recipient clicks afterwards, they see "Invitation revoked" and are directed back to . If you issue two pending invitations to the same email, the first one accepted wins; the second becomes invalid. This is rarely a problem in practice but can be confusing if both invitations land in the inbox at once. Cancel the older one before issuing a new one. What can go wrong - SMTP not configured — the invitation is created but no email is sent. The page surfaces a "SMTP not configured" banner; ask a Super Admin to fix the environment variables. Until that's done, you can manually copy the token from the audit log and DM the link to the recipient. - Email rejected by recipient's mail server — rare; usually means their inbox is full or rejecting your sender domain. Ask them to whitelist your sender and try again. - Recipient never receives — typical spam-filter problem. Have them search their spam folder and mark the sender as safe. Promoting a member to admin Edit the member from the Members page; flip the role from "member" to "admin"; save. The audit log records the change. The promoted member doesn't need to sign in again — their next page load picks up the new role. You can promote anyone who's already a member of your league. You can't promote someone who isn't yet a member — invite them first, then promote. Demoting an admin to member Same flow in reverse. Demotion takes effect on the next page load. There must always be at least one admin per league — the platform won't let you demote the last admin.

title: Editing members
summary: Update a member's display name, team name, email, or points deduction. Remove or reactivate members.
body: The Members page lists every member of your league with inline edit affordances for each row. Some fields apply to that league only; others propagate to every league the member belongs to. What's editable Per-membership (only affects this league) - Display name — what shows in standings, the leaderboard, the digest. Defaults to whatever FPL returns; you can override. - Team name — the FPL team name. Defaults to whatever FPL returns; you can override (e.g. to censor an offensive name). - Points deduction per gameweek — a per-week penalty applied to this member in this league. House-rule mechanism for fining someone who misses a deadline, fails to send a digest, etc. Defaults to 0. - Role — Member or Admin. See Inviting members for the constraints. - Active status — Active or Inactive. Inactive members don't appear in standings but their data is preserved. Cross-membership (affects every league the user is in) - Email — changing the email here changes it on the underlying UserAccount, which affects every league the user is a member of. Be deliberate — see the warning below. Updating a member's email rewires their entire account on the platform. If they're in three leagues, all three will now use the new email for magic-link sign-in. Confirm with the member before changing it, and prefer asking them to update it themselves via their profile (if/when that surface exists) over doing it from admin. Removing a member Two flavours: - Soft remove (deactivate) — flip Active to Inactive. The member disappears from standings but everything is preserved. You can reactivate later. This is the right choice if someone goes on a long break. - Hard remove — actually delete the LeagueMembership row. The member is gone from your league. Their UserAccount and any other league memberships are unaffected. The audit log records the removal. Hard remove is destructive in the sense that the in-league history (transfers, captain picks per GW) becomes inaccessible from your league's pages. The FPL data is still on FPL's servers — but the app no longer fetches it for this member. Reversing a hard remove is a re-invitation, not a reactivation. Points deduction The points deduction is a per-week subtraction. Set it to 2, and every gameweek for this member is recorded with . Set it back to 0 to stop deducting. Common uses: - A late-deadline penalty applied for the rest of the season ("you missed deadline = -2/wk for 5 weeks"). - A house rule like "if you don't pay your league fee, -1/wk until you do". Deductions appear as a small badge on the member's standings row and are logged in the audit trail. What you CAN'T edit - The member's FPL Manager ID. Once linked, the Manager ID is the connection to FPL's API; changing it would break their FPL history. If a member changes which FPL team they play, you have to hard-remove and re-invite them with the new Manager ID. - Anything about their FPL team selections (captain, transfers, chip usage). The app reads those from FPL; you can't write back. - Their data from other leagues they're in. Each LeagueMembership is separate; this page only edits this league's view.

title: Sending the weekly digest
summary: Trigger a GW-summary email to every member with a configured email address.
body: The weekly digest is a one-click email that summarises the just-completed gameweek for your league. It covers the GW winner, loser, best and worst captain, biggest bench waste, and an AI-generated per-manager paragraph that flavours the stats with whatever tone you've set on your digest prompt. Required configuration Before you can send a digest, three things must be set up at the platform level: | Environment variable | Why | |---|---| | | The outbound mail server. | | | Usually 587 for STARTTLS. | | / | Auth credentials. | | | The sender displayed in the email. | If any are missing, the Digest admin page shows a red "SMTP not configured" banner and the Send button is disabled. Ask a Super Admin to fix the environment variables. You'll also want set to your deployment's public URL so the email footer links back to the right place. How the digest is composed The digest has four parts: 1. Headline summary — GW winner, loser, league average, best captain, worst captain, biggest bench waste. 2. Full league table — every member's GW score and total, sorted by GW score. 3. Per-manager narratives — for each member with an email and ≥1 GW score, the AI generates a 2-3 sentence paragraph referencing their actual stats, in whatever tone you've configured on the digest prompt. 4. System notes — chips played, double-gameweek flags, anything notable about the GW itself. Sending Sidebar → Admin → Digest. The page shows the most recent successful send, the GW it covered, and the current configuration status. The button is disabled if SMTP isn't configured or if the AI provider (Groq) is unconfigured. Hover the disabled button for the specific reason. On click, the app: 1. Reads the current GW from the FPL API. 2. Checks the digest cache — if this GW's content has already been generated, reuse it (saves AI tokens). 3. Otherwise, generate fresh narratives (one call per manager with an email, sequential with a 1-second gap to stay within Groq rate limits). 4. Cache the result against the GW number. 5. Send the email to every member's configured email address, all BCC'd. On success: a green banner shows the number of recipients and the GW summary. On failure: a red banner with the actual error from the SMTP or Groq provider. What members receive A single BCC'd email per send. Each recipient sees only their own address in the To field and the league's sender in From. Members without a configured email on their LeagueMembership are silently skipped — they're not in the recipient list at all. The email is HTML with a plain-text fallback. The HTML uses your league's name and logo (if set) in the header. Clicking Send twice in a row sends the same content twice — there's no de-duplication. The digest cache only saves on AI generation cost; it doesn't block the second send from going out. If you accidentally double-send, apologise in the group chat and move on. When to send There's no schedule — you trigger manually. The most common cadence is "Monday or Tuesday after the final fixture of the gameweek, once the points have stabilised". Sending too early means provisional bonus points and final scores may differ from what's in the email; sending too late dilutes the value. If you forget for a week, that's fine — the next send picks up the most recent completed GW, not any of the missed ones. The platform has no "send for GW X retroactively" affordance. What if generation fails The most common failures: - Groq rate-limit (429) — too many tokens consumed in the past minute. Wait a minute and retry. The page surfaces the actual Groq error message. - Groq daily quota exhausted — the free tier has a daily cap. Wait until it resets (24-hour rolling window). - SMTP timeout — the mail server didn't respond. Check the server's status, try again. Failures don't burn the cache — if the first attempt failed midway, retrying picks up from where it left off (re-uses any narratives that did generate successfully).

title: Audit log
summary: Every administrative action in your league, who did it, and when. Read-only.
body: The Audit Log is the immutable record of every administrative action in your league. Settings changes, member edits, role promotions, invitations issued, digests sent, suspensions imposed — they all appear here with the actor, the target, the timestamp, and a JSON diff of what changed. What's logged Every mutation that goes through a or authorisation gate writes an . Read-only operations (viewing standings, opening the audit log itself) don't produce events. Examples of what you'll see: | Action | When it appears | |---|---| | | Settings page Save — includes before/after diff per changed field. | | | Promoting / demoting a member. | | | An invitation accepted, a member synced from FPL, a manual add. | | | A member marked inactive or hard-removed. | | | Invite-by-email button clicked. | | | Cancel-invitation button clicked. | | | Send-digest button clicked, with recipient count. | | / | Super Admin actions. Visible because they affect your league. | | | One-time entry from the initial 002 multi-league migration. | What's in each row - Timestamp — ISO 8601 UTC. - Actor — the email of the user who performed the action, OR for the one-time platform migration entries, OR for auto-actions like FPL sync runs. - Action — the dotted-namespace action key. - Target kind / id — what the action affected (e.g. , ). - Details — JSON payload with whatever the action recorded. For this is a before/after diff per changed field; for it's the recipient email and role. Filtering and search The page supports: - Filter by action — show only to audit settings changes, or only to count weekly sends. - Filter by actor — show only actions taken by a specific admin email. - Date range — start / end timestamps. - Full-text search — matches against the JSON blob. Why this exists For leagues with multiple admins, the audit log is the source of truth when "who changed X" comes up. It's the only mechanism that connects mutations to actors with a timestamp. Without it, mutations are anonymous in retrospect. For single-admin leagues, the log is mostly self-incrimination — it's a record of what you did and when. Still useful for "did I send the digest yet this week" type questions. You cannot delete or edit an audit event. If a bad event was logged (e.g. you accidentally promoted the wrong person), the corrective action also gets logged. The trail is complete by design — it's safe to share screenshots without redaction concerns. What the audit log does NOT contain - Page views — no read-action logging. Visiting the standings page or reading this manual doesn't produce events. - API requests — the audit is at the action level, not the HTTP level. One Save click that updates three fields = one event, not three. - Member-facing actions — when a member transfers a player or changes their captain, that happens on the FPL side. The audit log only sees app-level admin actions.

title: When a league is suspended
summary: What you and your members see when a Super Admin suspends the league, and what happens to your data.
body: A Super Admin can suspend a league at any time, with an optional reason. Suspension is a deliberate, recoverable state — not a deletion. The data is preserved exactly as it was; only access is gated. What members see When your league is suspended, every member who navigates to a page sees a full-page banner: > This league is suspended > > [optional reason from the Super Admin] > > Contact your league admin or the platform operator for details. The actual page content (standings, charts, members table, admin sub-shell) is NOT rendered. It exists in the database; the route handler short-circuits the render at the layout level. The sidebar still works — they can navigate to other leagues they belong to, or to platform-scoped pages like . They just can't enter this league's surfaces. What you (the League Admin) see Same banner. Suspension applies to admins too. You can't change settings, invite members, send digests, or read the audit log of a suspended league from the per-league admin sub-shell. You can still: - Read the Audit log entry that recorded the suspension, by sorting your league's audit by — accessible from the platform Super Admin view (visible to them only). - See the league listed on your /my-admin page if you administer multiple leagues, with a "Suspended" chip and the deep-link buttons disabled. What's preserved Everything. Memberships, audit events, league settings, digest cache, slug history — none of it is touched by suspension. The state is purely access-control. When the Super Admin reinstates the league, every surface lights up exactly as it was. No data is lost. Why a league might be suspended The Super Admin's call, but typical reasons: - The league's mini-league has been deleted on the FPL side, so member sync no longer works. - The platform operator needs to perform maintenance affecting that specific league. - The league has become inactive (no logins for months) and is being parked. - A house-rules dispute that's escalated to the platform level (rare). The Super Admin can include a public reason that surfaces on the banner. Or they can suspend silently with no reason. What to do as an admin If your league is suspended and you don't know why: 1. Check the audit log via the Super Admin — they can see the suspension event including any reason. 2. Reach out to the Super Admin — the banner says "contact your league admin or the platform operator". They are the only ones who can reinstate. If suspension is unexpected, ask first whether reinstatement is straightforward (e.g. you fix the issue that caused it) or whether it's a longer-term decision. This app deliberately doesn't expose league deletion as a normal operation — there's no "delete this league" button anywhere. Suspension is the cool-down mechanism. If a league truly needs to go away forever, that's a platform-operator database operation, not an in-app action.
